packets.key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the credit-card autopay-minimum option reduced minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, because nudged users set autopay only slightly above the minimum and some lost automatic payment protection entirely.
packets.methodology: Field experiment (RCT) on live credit card accounts with 6-month follow-up on payment behavior and debt.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly answers the brief's central question in the right setting: a consumer financial-product nudge changed nominal enrollment/behavior without moving the outcome that matters (debt/savings amount), and worsened outcomes for liquidity-constrained users — the strongest evidence for the support team's 'vanity enrolment' worry.
limitations: credit card debt paydown, not savings accumulation
single nudge design (shrouding), not a direct opt-in/opt-out/active-choice comparison
packets.relevance_reason: On-domain consumer financial nudge study showing default/nudge effects on nominal behavior diverge from substantive outcomes, directly contradicting the 'defaults always help' premise.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: In three experiments (including a representative five-country European sample, n=4207), default nudges strongly shift risk-taking with medium-to-large effect sizes, but a default nudge — and especially a refused default — lowers users' rating of the advice received, mediated by perceived wealth-manager honesty; how the default is framed and presented also shifts the amount invested.
packets.methodology: Three behavioral experiments, including a large representative multi-country EU sample, on default nudges in investment/advice settings.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly informs both open decisions: it shows a preset level's framing can anchor the amount chosen, and it gives EU consumer evidence on exactly when a default starts to read as manipulative and damage trust — the reputational risk the brief flags.
limitations: investment/wealth-management context rather than round-up savings specifically
no 6-12 month persistence measure, single-session experiments
packets.relevance_reason: EU consumer-financial experimental evidence directly on framing/anchoring of default levels and on perceived manipulation, matching the brief's regulatory concern almost exactly.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults increased campaign donations by over $43 million but also increased refund requests by almost $3 million, with larger effects on smaller, less-experienced donors who did not adjust the amount they donated to compensate.
packets.methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design exploiting different roll-out timing of prechecked recurring-donation boxes across 2020 U.S. campaign websites; large-scale transaction data.
packets.why_it_matters: A directly analogous consumer digital-choice-architecture default shows real enrollment gains alongside real regret/withdrawal signals concentrated among inexperienced users — the closest empirical evidence for the support team's disengagement and complaint concern about opt-out enrollment.
limitations: political donations, not savings behavior
no direct long-term retention measure beyond refund requests
U.S. setting, not EU regulatory context
packets.relevance_reason: Quantified evidence of both the enrollment-boosting power and distributional harm of a pre-checked recurring default in a real consumer digital product, closely mirroring the round-up feature's opt-out risk.
packets.title: Dark defaults: How choice architecture steers political campaign donations
packets.abstract: In the months before the 2020 U.S. election, several political campaign websites added prechecked boxes (defaults), automatically making all donations into recurring weekly contributions unless donors unchecked them. Since these changes occurred at different times for different campaigns, we use a staggered difference-in-differences design to measure the causal effects of defaults on donors' behavior. We estimate that defaults increased campaign donations by over $43 million while increasing requested refunds by almost $3 million. The weekly default only impacted weekly recurring donations, and not other donations, suggesting that donors may not have intended to make weekly donations. The longer defaults were displayed, the more money campaigns raised through weekly donations. Donors did not compensate by changing the amount they donated. We found that the default had a larger impact on smaller donors and on donors who had no prior experience with defaults, causing them to start more chains and donate a larger proportion of their money through weekly recurring donations.
packets.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

packets.key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million taxi tipping decisions finds 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost (friction complementarity), and a counterfactual added menu option captures 69% of achievable consumer welfare gain at only 5.4% revenue cost.
packets.methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on 8.6 million real transactions plus an independent stated-preference survey of preferences.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a rigorous, transferable method for reasoning about the round-up multiplier menu decision: how a preset level's design trades off consumer welfare against provider revenue, and how much of default adherence is genuine preference versus friction — directly useful for choosing and defending the 1x/2x/5x menu.
limitations: tipping decisions on a ride-hailing app, not a savings product
one-shot payment choice rather than an enrolled, ongoing savings behavior
packets.relevance_reason: A methodologically strong consumer digital-choice-architecture study whose menu-design and welfare-cost framework transfers directly to the round-up multiplier decision.
packets.title: Defaults and Decisions: Choice Architecture and Consumer Opt-Out
packets.abstract:
Why do consumers accept defaults (preset or suggested options)? This paper estimates a structural model that disentangles two frictions underlying default adherence: a deviation cost (the disutility when the final choice differs from the consumer’s ideal) and an opt-out cost (the effort to override the default). I estimate the model on 8.6 million tipping decisions from NYC Yellow taxi trips. A stated-preference survey identifies consumer tipping preferences independently of defaults. The central finding is friction complementarity: 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of both frictions; remove either friction and the remaining one alone cannot sustain default adherence. Structural parameters are approximately stable when default options change, consistent with defaults channeling behavior through choice frictions rather than reshaping preferences. Counterfactual analysis shows that adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20%–25%–30% menu captures 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
 This paper was accepted by Dube, Jean-Pierre, marketing.
 Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05272 .

packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for 'downstream' default effects, showing default effects on later consumer behavior depend on time course of choice/consumption, antecedent preferences, and salience of trade-offs, and are inconsistent across studies.
packets.methodology: Theoretical review/conceptual synthesis (taxonomy and framework), Consumer Psychology Review. Abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives the moderator variables (time course, prior preferences, salience) that should shape how we measure persistence at 6-12 months and who a default helps versus hurts — directly usable as a measurement checklist rather than a design choice.
limitations: conceptual/taxonomic, not a quantitative meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes
not specific to financial products
packets.relevance_reason: The clearest on-domain review of when and why default effects persist or fade downstream, filling the brief's request for a synthesis paper.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with the effect still visible 15+ months after rollout.
packets.methodology: Difference-in-differences analysis of the real-world DMA rollout across iOS and Android devices; large-scale usage data.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest large-scale, EU-regulatory, persistence-tested evidence on how forced/active choice compares to defaults — directly informs whether an active-choice onboarding step for the round-up feature would produce durable behavior change rather than a one-off bump.
limitations: mobile browser choice, not a financial savings product
does not measure amount saved or contribution levels
packets.relevance_reason: A real EU regulatory active-choice intervention with quantified, persistent effects — the strongest available evidence for the active-choice comparison criterion.
packets.title: The Effect of Choice Screens on Mobile Browser Usage: Evidence from the EU Digital Markets Act
packets.abstract: Can active choice mitigate the effects of preset defaults? We study this question using a difference-in-differences design around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions. We find large effects, with notable differences across platforms: from 15 months after the mandate onward, Firefox usage was 113 percent higher on iOS and 12 percent higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual. This gap is consistent with rollout differences, as Android showed choice screens primarily on new devices, whereas iOS also showed them on existing devices.Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.
packets.tldr: Large effects are found around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions, with notable differences across platforms.

packets.key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft alerts cut unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in market-wide annual savings, though achieving less than half of the potential avoidable savings.
packets.methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments at major UK banks; abstract-only for statistics.
packets.why_it_matters: The closest real consumer-banking analog of automatic enrollment producing measurable behavioral savings, setting a benchmark for what an opt-out round-up design could realistically achieve and its shortfall from the ceiling.
limitations: studies overdraft alerts, not savings contributions
no data on enrollment persistence or engagement depth over 6-12 months for the feature itself
packets.relevance_reason: A large-scale UK consumer-bank field experiment on automatic enrollment gives a directly comparable effect-size benchmark in the same industry and regulatory environment.
packets.title: Sending Out an SMS: Automatic Enrollment Experiments for Overdraft Alerts
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT At‐scale field experiments at major U.K. banks show that automatic enrollment into “just‐in‐time” text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft and unpaid item charges 17% to 19% and arranged overdraft charges 4% to 8%, implying annual market‐wide savings of £170 million to £240 million. Incremental benefits from “early‐warning” alerts are statistically insignificant, although economically significant effects are not ruled out. Prior to the experiments, over half of overdrafts could have been avoided by using lower‐cost liquidity available in savings and credit card accounts. Alerts help consumers achieve less than half of these potential savings.

packets.key_finding: In an RCT with 220 participants, all tested nudges - including default options - significantly reduced willingness to contribute to voluntary pension savings relative to a control group, contrary to prevailing international evidence, with the largest backfire from positive-narrative and default-option nudges.
packets.methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey (N=220) testing social norms, framing, default options, and narrative nudges on Chinese voluntary pension-saving decisions.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise enrollment or contribution, a rare empirical counter-example the brief explicitly asked us to weigh against the 'defaults always help' assumption.
limitations: small online survey sample (n=220) measuring stated willingness rather than real financial behavior
Chinese cultural/institutional context differs from an EU consumer app
voluntary pension product rather than a liquid consumer savings app
packets.relevance_reason: The clearest available contradiction of the 'defaults always help' premise, directly answering the brief's explicit request for counter-evidence.
packets.title: When Nudges Backfire: The Effect of Social Norms, Framing Effects, and Default Options on the Pension Saving Decisions in China
packets.abstract: This study investigates the impact of behavioral nudgessocial norms, loss aversion framing, default options, and positive narrativeon voluntary pension saving decisions in China. Using a randomized controlled trial administered via an online survey with 220 participants, we examine how these interventions influence both the willingness to contribute and the proportion of income allocated to pension savings. Contrary to prevailing international evidence, our results indicate that all nudges significantly reduce willingness to contribute relative to a control group, with the most substantial backfire effects observed for positive narrative and default option nudges. Furthermore, we identify important heterogeneity effects across income groups and emphasize the moderating roles of education, gender, and financial motivation. These findings underscore the critical importance of cultural, institutional, and individual factors in the design and implementation of behavioral interventions. Policy measures tailored to specific demographic segments and focused on financial education and trust-building are recommended.
packets.venue: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences

packets.key_finding: Synthesizes household-finance evidence on how choice architecture, product design, defaults, and disclosure shape savings and other financial decisions, situating default effects among a broader intervention toolkit.
packets.methodology: Narrative review/NBER chapter summarizing empirical regularities and intervention evidence in household finance.
packets.why_it_matters: Provides the review-level synthesis of choice-architecture and default evidence the brief asked for, giving broader context for benchmarking both design decisions.
limitations: broad overview rather than a study with its own effect sizes
covers household finance generally, not round-up savings or EU fintech specifically
synthesizes largely employer-plan and classic literature
packets.relevance_reason: Supplies the review/meta-level synthesis of default and choice-architecture evidence the brief explicitly wants represented.
packets.title: Behavioral Household Finance
packets.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of household finance. The first part summarizes key facts regarding household financial behavior, emphasizing empirical regularities that are inconsistent with the standard classical economic model and discussing extensions of the classical model and explanations grounded in behavioral economics that can account for the observed patterns. This part covers five topics: consumption and savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance. The second part addresses interventions that firms, governments, and other parties deploy to shape household financial outcomes: education and information, peer effects and social influence, product design, advice and disclosure, choice architecture, and interventions that directly target prices or quantities.

packets.key_finding: Field experiments show 'active choice' meaningfully changes behavior relative to no intervention, and a novel 'enhanced active choice' variant that highlights losses from the non-preferred option can approach the effectiveness of automatic enrolment.
packets.methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments comparing opt-out defaults, plain active choice, and enhanced active choice on behavior-change outcomes.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly answers whether active choice can capture most of the enrolment benefit of a default without an opt-out, exactly the comparison the brief needs for the entry-design decision, and proposes a concrete design to test.
limitations: field experiments are in medication adherence and general savings contexts, not a round-up banking app
older study (2011), predates current fintech/regulatory context
abstract does not fully quantify enhanced-active-choice effect sizes
packets.relevance_reason: The origin study of active choice and enhanced active choice as an alternative to opt-out defaults, the mechanism the entry decision needs evidence on (C6).
packets.title: Enhanced active choice: A new method to motivate behavior change
packets.abstract: Abstract High rates of medication non‐adherence have significant public health and economic consequences. In other contexts such as savings behavior, opt‐out policies, in which the alternative preferred by the policy maker is made the default, have gotten great traction but may not be feasible in health care settings. After reviewing previous applications, we present a series of studies, including two field experiments, that test the effectiveness of an alternative, ‘active choice’ policy in which there is no default, but decision makers are required to make a choice (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, & Metrick, 2009; Spital, 1993, 1995). In addition, we propose and test a modified version of active choice, that we call ‘enhanced active choice’ that favors one alternative by highlighting losses incumbent in the in the non‐preferred alternative. We recommend Enhanced Active Choice as a complement to automatic enrollment or when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical.

alternates.key_finding: A field experiment with a consumer financial-management platform found payment reminders cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
alternates.methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil, abstract-only for design details.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly supports the support team's worry that a uniform nudge/default can help most users while making a vulnerable subgroup worse off — exactly the distributional risk the brief says we must check before defaulting everyone in.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrolment defaults or contribution-level anchoring
credit card/overdraft fee context rather than a round-up savings pot
no measure of long-run persistence beyond the fee outcomes reported
alternates.relevance_reason: Strong consumer-fintech evidence of heterogeneous, sometimes harmful, effects from a well-intentioned behavioural intervention, directly relevant to the brief's distributional-risk criterion.
alternates.title: Side Effects of Nudging: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in the Credit Card Market
alternates.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the direct and indirect effects of nudging, by means of a field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil. Reminders for upcoming credit card payments reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14%, but increased overdraft fees in checking accounts by 9%. The unintended effect is concentrated in users with a history of overdraft use. These users experienced a net increase of 5% in total fees, while the rest experienced savings of 15%. The results provide clear insights for nudge design: like any policy action, nudges can have side effects, and one size may not fit all.

alternates.key_finding: Randomly assigning default enrolment into a salary-linked savings account raised participation by 40 percentage points, equivalent to a 50% matching incentive, driven by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of thinking through savings scenarios rather than by trust in the payer, with effects on savings attitudes persisting after the study ended.
alternates.methodology: Randomized field experiment among salaried employees in Afghanistan with follow-on interventions isolating mechanisms behind the default effect.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly tests why defaults work — present bias and cognitive cost, not employer-trust — speaking to the brief's core question of whether the default effect should be expected to transfer to a self-directed consumer app, and shows persistence of attitude change beyond the intervention.
limitations: salary-linked account for waged employees, a semi-employer-mediated setting rather than a fully self-directed consumer app
developing-country context differs from EU regulatory/liquidity context
abstract reports participation and attitude persistence, not amount saved
alternates.relevance_reason: Uniquely isolates the psychological mechanism behind default effects rather than employer trust, addressing whether the effect transfers to our non-employer setting.
alternates.title: Why Do Defaults Affect Behavior? Experimental Evidence from Afghanistan
alternates.abstract: We report on an experiment examining why default options impact behavior. By randomly assigning employees to different varieties of a salary-linked savings account, we find that default enrollment increases participation by 40 percentage points—an effect equivalent to providing a 50 percent matching incentive. We then use a series of experimental interventions to differentiate between explanations for the default effect, which we conclude is driven largely by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of thinking through different savings scenarios. Default assignment also changes employees’ attitudes toward saving, and makes them more likely to actively decide to save after the study concludes. (JEL C93, D14, D91, O12)

alternates.key_finding: People generally approve of financial nudges/interventions, rating them positively on approval, benefit, ethics and likelihood-of-use (with manipulation reverse-coded), with stronger approval for System-2-style and savings-framed interventions regardless of whether a bank is the messenger.
alternates.methodology: Pre-registered online survey experiment with 2,100 representative Australian respondents shown 36 hypothetical financial-intervention scenarios varying transparency, framing and System type.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly tests whether consumers perceive bank-issued savings nudges as manipulative or acceptable, which is the reputational/dark-pattern risk the brief flags for the entry-design decision.
limitations: hypothetical scenarios rather than an actual enrolment decision
Australian sample, not EU
no measurement of enrolment or amount saved
alternates.relevance_reason: Provides direct consumer evidence on perceived manipulativeness of bank-proposed savings nudges, informing C5.
alternates.title: Do people like financial nudges?
alternates.abstract: Abstract Do people like financial nudges? To answer that question we conducted a pre-registered survey presenting people with 36 hypothetical scenarios describing financial interventions. We varied levels of transparency (i.e., explaining how the interventions worked), framing (interventions framed in terms of spending, or saving), and ‘System’ (interventions could target either System 1 or System 2). Participants were a random sample of 2,100 people drawn from a representative Australian population. All financial interventions were tested across six dependent variables: approval, benefit, ethics, manipulation, the likelihood of use, as well as the likelihood of use if the intervention were to be proposed by a bank. Results indicate that people generally approve of financial interventions, rating them as neutral to positive across all dependent variables (except for manipulation, which was reverse coded). We find effects of framing and System. People have strong and significant preferences for System 2 interventions, and interventions framed in terms of savings. Transparency was not found to have a significant impact on how people rate financial interventions. Financial interventions continue to be rated positive, regardless of the messenger. Looking at demographics, we find that participants who were female, younger, living in metro areas and earning higher incomes were most likely to favor financial interventions, and this effect is especially strong for those aged under 45. We discuss the implications for these results as applied to the financial sector.

alternates.key_finding: EU dark-pattern law protects biased consumers under an autonomy lens; the paper builds a taxonomy of six categories of autonomy violations to classify when pre-selected defaults and similar choice-architecture practices become regulable dark patterns.
alternates.methodology: Doctrinal/legal analysis mapping EU laws addressing dark patterns and proposing a normative classification; abstract-only.
alternates.why_it_matters: Gives the EU regulatory framework for distinguishing a helpful opt-out default from a legally and reputationally risky dark pattern, directly bearing on the entry-design decision's compliance exposure.
limitations: legal/normative analysis, not empirical
no effect sizes on enrolment or savings behavior
general online choice architecture, not a round-up savings feature specifically
alternates.relevance_reason: Provides the EU legal taxonomy for when a pre-selected default crosses into a dark pattern, central to the brief's reputational-risk concern.
alternates.title: Regulating Dark Patterns
alternates.abstract: Dark patterns have become increasingly pervasive in online choice architectures, encompassing practices like subscription traps, hiding information about fees, pre-selecting options by default, nagging, and drip pricing. Regulators around the world have started to express concerns that such practices are causing substantial consumer detriment. This Article focuses on the legal response to dark patterns in the European Union. It provides the first comprehensive mapping of European Union laws expressly addressing dark patterns. The Article argues that these laws protect biased consumers and adopt autonomy as a normative lens to assess dark patterns. Consequently, regulating dark patterns in European Union law means regulating for autonomy. This normative lens is under-researched. This Article addresses this gap in research with two principle contributions. First, it works out a specific conception of autonomous decision-making, rooted in the paradigm that providing consumers with information enables consumers to make an informed decision. Second, the Article offers a novel normative classification for dark patterns in online choice architectures. It develops a taxonomy encompassing six categories of autonomy violations, specifically tailored for the assessment and regulation of dark patterns that exploit consumer behavioral biases. These categories serve multiple purposes. They uncover and make explicit the autonomy violations addressed by existing European Union laws. They delineate the contentious line between acceptable influences on consumer decision-making and autonomy violations that may warrant regulation in online choice architectures. They also provide policymakers in the EU and elsewhere with a framework when deliberating the regulation of other instances of dark patterns.

alternates.key_finding: Using natural experiments with random assignment to default options in Medicare Part D, beneficiary passivity toward defaults is large, persistent, and strikingly insensitive to how bad the default option is; active-choice variation looks driven by transitory attention shocks rather than stable attentiveness.
alternates.methodology: Three natural experiments, including random assignment to default plan options, on Medicare Part D administrative data.
alternates.why_it_matters: Strong evidence that people do not self-correct out of bad defaults even when it costs them materially — a caution against assuming a good default choice will be actively corrected if wrong, and evidence that 'active choosers' are not a stable, identifiable segment.
limitations: health insurance/drug plan setting, not a consumer financial savings product
no employer- or app-based enrollment mechanism comparable to ours
alternates.relevance_reason: Closest non-employer analogue on default persistence and the limits of active choice, though the domain (health insurance) is not the brief's financial-product setting.
alternates.title: The Behavioral Foundations of Default Effects: Theory and Evidence from Medicare Part D
alternates.abstract: We show in two natural experiments that default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization of low-income beneficiaries. The implications of this phenomenon for welfare and optimal policy depend on the sensitivity of passivity to the value of the default option. Using random assignment to default options, we show that beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive, even when enrolling in the default option would result in substantial drug consumption losses. A third natural experiment suggests that variation in active choice is driven by random transitory shocks rather than the inherent attentiveness of some beneficiaries.
